quote: Not only is this state of knowledge a plausible one, it is the state of knowledge possessed by e.g. Sadi Carnot, who, working strictly from within the caloric theory of heat, developed the principle of the Carnot cycle—a heat engine of maximum efficiency, whose existence implies the Second Law of Thermodynamics. This in 1824, when kinetics was a highly developed science.
content: Carnot is the wrong example, because Carnot conceived the identity the essay says his state of knowledge made inconceivable. His posthumous notes, published by his brother in 1878, record his abandonment of caloric: “heat is nothing else than motive power, or rather motion which has changed form,” with an estimate of the mechanical equivalent of heat about fifteen years before Joule. He got there from the same knowledge of engines and mechanics the essay attributes to him. The kinetic theory was also not a late arrival; Daniel Bernoulli derived the gas laws from molecular motion in 1738, and caloric won the eighteenth century not because kineticists could not imagine the reduction but because caloric explained more at the time (Laplace’s correction to the speed of sound, latent heat, radiant heat), as Chang’s Inventing Temperature (2004, a book with no DOI) documents. And “still earlier, the main theory of heat was ‘Phlogiston!’” is the recurring error of this book (Book I’s annotations counted it): phlogiston was a theory of combustion and calcination, not of heat, and coexisted with elemental-fire and material-heat theories rather than preceding them.

quote: To Richard Feynman, armed with specific knowledge of how to derive equations about heat from equations about motion, this idea is not only inconceivable, but so wildly inconsistent as to make one’s head explode.
content: Heat is not identical to kinetic energy, and Feynman knew it. Heat, in thermodynamics, is energy in transit across a boundary by thermal contact, a process quantity; the state quantity is internal energy, which for anything but a monatomic ideal gas includes potential energy of intermolecular forces, vibrational and rotational modes, and, for radiation, no molecular motion at all. Thermal radiation carries heat through a vacuum in which nothing moves; a spin system can have negative absolute temperature. The identification “heat is molecular motion” is a nineteenth-century slogan that survives in popular writing, and the essay’s Feynman finds its denial “wildly inconsistent” only if he has redefined heat as mean kinetic energy, which is Thinker 1’s move of settling the question by choosing a definition. This matters for the essay’s thesis, that detailed knowledge of a reduction makes the alternative inconceivable. The detailed knowledge here shows the reduction to be partial and the identity to be false as stated, and what becomes inconceivable is not “heat is not motion” but “thermal phenomena have no microphysical account,” a much weaker claim that nobody since caloric has denied.

quote: It appears to me that “water” is being used in two different senses in these two paragraphs—one in which the word “water” refers to what we type into the Science Interpreter, and one in which “water” refers to what we get out of the Science Interpreter when we type “water” into it.
content: The two senses have names, and the person who gave them their most developed form is the philosopher the next four essays are written against. Kripke’s Naming and Necessity (1980) distinguishes the epistemic status of “water is H2O” (a posteriori) from its modal status (necessary), which is what Putnam’s two paragraphs are saying; Chalmers’s two-dimensional semantics (Chalmers, “The Components of Content,” 2002, and The Conscious Mind, 1996, ch. 2) formalizes the difference as the primary intension (what “water” picks out considered as a function from ways the world might turn out) and the secondary intension (what it picks out given how the world actually is), and “what we type in” versus “what we get out” is a serviceable gloss of that pair. The essay’s “I believe the above has already been said as well?” is right, and the essay’s further reading of Putnam, that after the discovery water is “automatically redefined to mean H2O,” is not what Putnam said: his claim is that “water” rigidly designated the local stuff all along and that chemistry revealed what it had been designating, with no redefinition. The essay reinvents the framework it needs in order to argue with Chalmers, and then, in Zombie Responses, uses the Twin Earth analogy as its decisive move without noticing that Kripke argued, in the same lectures, that the analogy fails for exactly the case of consciousness.
